Grid Resolution and its Interaction with Boundaries\n\n**Grid spec hierarchy** (`/workspace/autofdtd/src/autofdtd/grid/specs.py`):\n```\nGridSpec\n├── grid_x: AxisGridSpec (UniformGrid | CustomGridBoundaries | CustomGrid | AutoGrid)\n├── grid_y: AxisGridSpec\n├── grid_z: AxisGridSpec\n├── wavelength: float | None\n└── layer_refinement_specs: tuple[LayerRefinementSpec, ...]\n```\n\n**Resolved grid**:\n```python\nclass ResolvedGrid(TaggedModel):\n    center: Vec3\n    size: Vec3\n    x: ResolvedGridAxis  # boundaries: tuple[float, ...], num_cells\n    y: ResolvedGridAxis\n    z: ResolvedGridAxis\n```\n\n**`ResolvedGridAxis` properties**:\n- `num_cells` - number of primal cells on axis\n- `cell_sizes` - per-cell widths\n- `min_step`, `max_step` - extreme cell sizes\n\n**Grid-boundary interaction**:\n- `compile_boundary_spec()` takes `grid_spacing: float | tuple[float, float, float]` parameter\n- Per-axis grid spacing is used to compute PML/ABC coefficients:\n  ```python\n  sigma_value = polynomial_profile(params.sigma_min, params.sigma_max, params.sigma_order, fraction)\n  damping_rate = max(0.0, sigma_value / kappa_value + alpha_value)\n  attenuation_value = math.exp(-damping_rate * dt / grid_spacing)\n  ```\n- The `CompiledBoundarySpec` stores `pml_grid_spacing: tuple[float, float, float]` for runtime PML application\n\n---\n\n### 4. Existing Chunk Decomposition Logic\n\n**There is NONE.** The `CompiledSimulation` dataclass has no chunk decomposition:\n\n```python\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass CompiledSimulation:\n    simulation_ir: SimulationIR\n    resolved_grid: ResolvedGrid\n    runtime_controls: CompiledRuntimeControls\n    scene_coefficients: CompiledSceneCoefficients\n    compiled_sources: CompiledSources\n    compiled_monitors: CompiledMonitors\n    compiled_boundaries: CompiledBoundaries\n```\n\nThe pipeline is:\n```\nSimulation → compile_simulation() → CompiledSimulation (monolithic)\n```\n\n**What exists that WOULD be relevant for chunks**:\n- `BoundaryMode` enum has `PERIODIC`, `BLOCH`, `PEC`, `PMC`, `ABC`, `PML`, `STABLE_PML`, `ABSORBER`\n- `exchange_kind` per axis: `\"periodic\" | \"bloch\" | \"reflective\" | \"abc\" | \"pml\" | \"mixed\"`\n- `periodic_axes`, `bloch_axes` tuples that identify which axes need cross-chunk communication\n- `stage_order` tuple for update ordering: `(\"electric_boundary\", \"magnetic_boundary\", \"electric_abc\", \"magnetic_abc\", \"electric_pml\", \"magnetic_pml\")`\n\n---\n\n### 6. Each chunk is a contiguous region of space &mdash; a line, rectangle, or parallelepiped for 1d/2d/3d Cartesian geometries, or an annular section in a cylindrical geometry&mdash;whose sizes are automatically determined by `libmeep.` In [parallel calculations](Parallel_Meep.md), each chunk is assigned, in its entirety, to precisely one process &mdash; that is, no chunk exists partly on one processor and partly on another.\n7\t\n8\tMany internal operations in Meep consist of looping over points in the\n9\t[Yee grid](Yee_Lattice.md), generally performing some operation involving the field\n10\tcomponents and material parameters at each point.\n11\tIn principle, this involves nested `for` loops; in practice,\n12\tit is complicated by several factors, including the following:\n13\t\n14\t+ For calculations that [exploit symmetry](Exploiting_Symmetry.md), only a\n15\tportion of the full grid is actually stored in memory, and obtaining values\n16\tfor field components at a point that *isn't* stored requires a tricky\n17\tprocedure discussed below.\n18\t\n19\t+ Similarly, for Bloch-periodic geometries, only grid points in the unit cell\n20\tare stored, but we may want the fields at a point lying outside the unit cell,\n21\tagain requiring a bit of a shell game to process correctly.\n22\t\n23\t+ Because of the staggered nature of the [Yee grid](Yee_Lattice.md),\n24\t\"looping over grid points\" can mean multiple things &mdash; are we visiting\n25\tonly **E**-field sites, or only **H**-field sites, or both? Either\n26\tway, obtaining a full set of field-component values at any one grid point\n27\tnecessarily involves a certain average over neighboring grid points.\n28\t\n29\tTo shield developers from the need to grapple with these complications\n30\twhen implementing loops over grid points, `libmeep` provides\n31\ta convenient routine called `loop_in_chunks` and a set of macros\n32\tthat take care of many of the above hassles. In particular, consecutive chunks are *not* necessarily adjacent.\n71\t\n72\t#### Chunk Statistics\n73\t\n74\tAs noted above, each chunk is a contiguous region of space defined\n75\tby a Cartesian product of intervals for each coordinate; to specify\n76\tthe extents of the chunk it thus suffices to specify the endpoints\n77\tof the interval for each coordinate, or equivalently the coordinates\n78\tof the lower-left and upper-right grid points in the chunk. For each\n79\tchunk, these are represented by `ivecs` named `is` and `ie`\n80\t(stored in the `fields_chunk` and `dft_chunk` structures).\n81\t\n82\tHere's an example of how this looks for chunk 3 in the figure above:\n83\t\n84\t<p align=\"center\"> <a href=\"../images/ChunkStatistics.png\"><img src=\"../images/ChunkStatistics.png\" style='height: 100%; width: 100%; object-fit: contain'/></a></p>\n85\t\n86\tIn this case we have `is=(29,-29)` and `ie=(39,-19)`.\n87\t\n88\t### Chunking in the Multiprocessor Case\n89\t\n90\tWhen running in parallel mode, each of the chunks identified for the\n91\tsingle-processor case may be further subdivided into new chunks which\n92\tcan be assigned to different processors.\n93\tFor example, on a run with 8 processors, the 9 chunks identified\n94\tin the single-processor case become 24 chunks:\n95\t\n96\t<p align=\"center\"> <a href=\"../images/Chunks_NP8.png\"><img src=\"../images/Chunks_NP8.png\" style='height: 100%; width: 100%; object-fit: contain'/></a></p>\n97\t\n98\tIn this image, grid points with different $z$ coordinates (different\n99\theights off the $xy$ plane) are handled by different processors,\n100\twhile points with the same $z$ coordinate but different colors\n101\tlive in different chunks. In this case, processes 0, 2, 5, and 7\n102\teach own 4 chunks, while processes 1, 3, 4, and 6 each own 2 chunks.\n103\t\n104\t## Symmetries\n105\t\n106\tMeep's approach to handling symmetries is discussed\n107\tfrom the user's perspective in [Exploiting Symmetry](Exploiting_Symmetry.md)\n108\tand from a high-level algorithmic perspective in [Computer Physics Communications, Vol. 181, pp. 687-702 (2010)](http://ab-initio.mit.edu/~oskooi/papers/Oskooi10.pdf).\n109\t\n110\tThe following is a brief synopsis of the implementation of this feature.\n111\t\n112\t+ The action of the symmetry group classifies grid points into *orbits,*\n113\t  sets of grid points that transform into one another under symmetry\n114\t  transformations. For example, in the figure with XY mirror symmetry below,\n115\t  the orbit of\n116\t  $\\mathbf{x}_a$ is $\\{\\mathbf{x}_a, \\mathbf{x}_b, \\mathbf{x}_c, \\mathbf{x}_d\\}$.\n117\t  Meep chooses one element from each orbit (the \"parent\" grid point)\n118\t  to serve as a representative of the orbit, with the remaining elements of\n119\t  the orbit classified as \"children\" equivalent to the parent under\n120\t  the group action.\n121\t  (Any point in the orbit could serve equally well as the parent;\n122\t   the convention in meep is to choose the point with the lowest (most negative)\n123\t   grid indices, i.e the point closest to the lower-left corner of the overall\n124\t   grid---$\\mathbf{x}_a$ in this case---but nothing depends on this particular choice.)\n125\t\n126\t+ For each orbit, field components are only stored for the parent, not for\n127\t  any children. This reduces memory requirements by a factor $M$,\n128\t  the number of points in each orbit, known in meep as the ``multiplicity''\n129\t  of the symmetry; for example, $M=2$ for a geometry with *Y*-mirror symmetry,\n130\t  $M=4$ for an *XY*-mirror symmetry, $M=N$ for an *N*-fold rotational\n131\t  symmetry, etc.\n132\t\n133\t+ Loops over grid points run only over parent points, i.e. points with field\n134\t  components stored in memory. However, each parent point is now visited\n135\t  $M$ times, once for each distinct symmetry transformation\n136\t  $\\mathcal{S}_m (m=1,\\cdots,M) $ in the symmetry group\n137\t  (including the identity transformation). On the $m$th visit to a given\n138\t  parent point $\\mathbf{x}_p$, we\n139\t\n140\t    **(1)** look up the components of the fields $\\mathbf{E}_p, \\mathbf{H}_p$\n141\t            stored in memory for $\\mathbf{x}_p$,\n142\t\n143\t    **(2)** apply the transformation $\\mathcal{S}_m$ to both the grid-point\n144\t            coordinates and the field components of the parent point to yield\n145\t            the coordinates and field components of the $m$th child point, i.e.\n146\t            $$       \\mathbf{x}_{cm} = \\mathcal{S}_m \\mathbf{x}_p,\n147\t              \\quad \\mathbf{E}_{cm} = \\mathcal{S}_m \\mathbf{E}_p,\n148\t              \\quad \\mathbf{H}_{cm} = \\mathcal{S}_m \\mathbf{H}_p.\n149\t            $$\n150\t           If the materials are anisotropic (i.e. the permittivity and/or permeability\n151\t           are tensors) we must transform those appropriately as well.\n152\t\n153\t    **(3)** use the coordinates and field components of the child point to carry\n154\t            out the operation in question.\n155\t\n156\t### Chunking in the Presence of Symmetries\n157\t\n158\tAs noted above, in the presence of symmetries only a portion of the\n159\tfull grid is actually stored in memory. For example, adding a $y$ mirror\n160\tsymmetry (symmetry under reflection about the $x$-axis) eliminates\n161\tpoints in the upper half-plane $(y>0)$; the points that remain are\n162\tnow subdivided into 6 chunks (in the single-processor case):\n163\t\n164\t<p align=\"center\"> <a href=\"../images/Chunks_YSymmetry.png\"><img src=\"../images/Chunks_YSymmetry.png\" style='height: 100%; width: 100%; object-fit: contain'/></a></p>\n165\t\n166\tAdding an $x$ mirror symmetry on top of this (so that now the geometry has\n167\tboth $x$ and $y$ mirror symmetry) reduces the number of stored grid points by an\n168\tadditional factor of 2; now the geometry is subdivided into just 4 chunks\n169\tin the single-processor case:\n170\t\n171\t<p align=\"center\"> <a href=\"../images/Chunks_XYSymmetry.png\"><img src=\"../images/Chunks_XYSymmetry.png\" style='height: 100%; width: 100%; object-fit: contain'/></a></p>\n172\t\n173\tIn these figures, points in shaded regions are \"children\" &mdash; that is, points\n174\tfor which Meep stores no field components, since they are related by symmetry\n175\tto \"parent\" points in the unshaded region. In the second figure we have\n176\tindicated one complete orbit: parent point $\\mathbf{x}_a$ is carried to\n177\tchild points $\\{\\mathbf{x}_b, \\mathbf{x}_c, \\mathbf{x}_d\\}$ under the\n178\toperations of the symmetry group.\n179\t\n180\t### Coordinates and Field Components of Symmetry-Reduced Points\n181\t\n182\tSymmetry transformations in `libmeep` are described by a class called\n183\tsimply `symmetry,` which offers class methods for transforming grid\n184\tpoints and field components:\n185\t\n186\t```c++\n187\t\n188\t  symmetry S = mirror(X,gv) + mirror(Y,gv);    // XY mirror symmetry\n189\t\n190\t  ivec iparent;                                // grid indices of parent point\n191\t  vec  rparent;                                // cartesian coordinates of parent point\n192\t\n193\t  ...\n194\t\n195\t  ivec ichild = S.transform(iparent, +1);      // grid indices of child point\n196\t   vec rchild = S.transform(rparent, +1);      // cartesian coordinates of child point\n197\t\n198\t  component cchild  = Ex;                      // desired field component at child point\n199\t  component cparent = S.transform(cchild, -1); // corresponding component at parent point\n200\t```\n201\t\n202\t## The `loop_in_chunks` Routine\n203\t\n204\tTo allow developers to implement loops over grid points without\n205\tstressing out over the various complications outlined above,\n206\tthe `fields` class in `libmeep` offers a convenient method called\n207\t`loop_in_chunks.`\n208\t\n209\tTo use this routine, you will first write a \"chunk-loop function\"\n210\twhich carries out some operation involving grid points and (optionally)\n211\tfield components at grid points. Then you pass your routine to\n212\t`loop_in_chunks` with some additional arguments customizing the\n213\ttype of loop you want (see below). Your loop function will then be\n214\tcalled once for every `chunk` in the problem---including both\n215\tchunks whose fields are present in memory, and those\n216\twhose aren't due to being eliminated by symmetry---with a long list\n217\tof arguments describing the chunk in question.\n218\t\n219\tThe body of your chunk-loop function will typically want to execute\n220\ta loop over all grid points in the chunk. This is facilitated by a host\n221\tof utility macros and API functions that operate on the arguments to your function\n222\tto yield quantities of interest: grid-point coordinates, field-component\n223\tvalues, etc.\n224\t\n225\t### The Chunk Loop Function\n226\t\n227\tThe chunk-loop function that you write and pass to `loop_in_chunks`\n228\thas the following prototype:\n229\t\n230\t```c++\n231\tvoid field_chunkloop(fields_chunk *fc, int ichunk, component cgrid, ivec is, ivec ie,\n232\t                     vec s0, vec s1, vec e0, vec e1, double dV0, double dV1,\n233\t                     ivec shift, std::complex<double> shift_phase,\n234\t\t             const symmetry &S, int sn, void *chunkloop_data);\n235\t```\n236\t\n237\tNotwithstanding this formidable-looking beast of a calling convention,\n238\tmost of the arguments here are things that you can blindly pass on to\n239\tAPI functions and convenience macros, which will return quantities whose\n240\tsignificance is easy to understand.\n241\t\n242\tHere's a skeleton chunk-loop function\n243\tthat executes a loop over all grid points in the chunk,\n244\tobtaining on each loop iteration both the integer indices and the cartesian\n245\tcoordinates of the child point, as well as values for a list\n246\tof field components of interest (specified before the loop in the\n247\tconstructor of `chunkloop_field_components`). You can fill in the rest of the loop body\n248\tto do whatever you want with `ichild,` `rchild,` and `data.values,` and the\n249\tresults will be identical whether or not you declare symmetries when\n250\tdefining your geometry. (Well, the results will be identical assuming\n251\tthe physical problem you're considering really is symmetric, which Meep [does not check](Exploiting_Symmetry.md).)\n252\t\n253\t```c++\n254\tvoid my_chunkloop(fields_chunk *fc, int ichunk, component cgrid, ivec is, ivec ie,\n255\t                  vec s0, vec s1, vec e0, vec e1, double dV0, double dV1,\n256\t                  ivec shift, std::complex<double> shift_phase,\n257\t\t          const symmetry &S, int sn, void *chunkloop_data)\n258\t{\n259\t  // some preliminary setup\n260\t  vec rshift(shift * (0.5*fc->gv.inva));  // shift into unit cell for PBC geometries\n261\t\n262\t  // prepare the list of field components to fetch at each grid point\n263\t  component components[] = {Ex, Hz};\n264\t  chunkloop_field_components data(fc, cgrid, shift_phase, S, sn, 2, components);\n265\t\n266\t  // loop over all grid points in chunk\n267\t  LOOP_OVER_IVECS(fc->gv, is, ie, idx)\n268\t   {\n269\t     // get grid indices and coordinates of parent point\n270\t     IVEC_LOOP_ILOC(gv, iparent);  // grid indices\n271\t     IVEC_LOOP_LOC(gv, rparent);   // cartesian coordinates\n272\t\n273\t     // apply symmetry transform to get grid indices and coordinates of child point\n274\t     ivec ichild = S.transform(iparent, sn) + shift;\n275\t     vec rchild = S.transform(rparent, sn) + rshift;\n276\t\n277\t     // fetch field components at child point\n278\t     data.update_values(idx);\n279\t     std::complex<double> Ex = data.values[0],\n280\t                          Hz = data.values[1];\n281\t   }\n282\t}\n283\t```\n284\t\n285\t## Is There a Version of `loop_in_chunks` for `dft_chunks`?\n286\t\n287\tNo, but the routine `process_dft_component()` in `src/dft.cpp` effectively\n288\timplements such a routine for a hard-coded set of operations on DFT\n289\tcomponents (namely: outputting to HDF5, fetching DFT array slices,\n290\tand computing mode-overlap coefficients).\n291\t\n292\t## How the Images were Created\n293\t\n294\tThe images above were obtained with the help of a simple C++ code\n295\tcalled `WriteChunkInfo` that calls `libmeep` API functions to\n296\tobtain info on the chunk structure of the 40&times;30 grid\n297\twe considered.
