Each chunk is a contiguous region of space &mdash; a line, rectangle, or parallelepiped for 1d/2d/3d Cartesian geometries, or an annular section in a cylindrical geometry&mdash;whose sizes are automatically determined by `libmeep.` In [parallel calculations](Parallel_Meep.md), each chunk is assigned, in its entirety, to precisely one process &mdash; that is, no chunk exists partly on one processor and partly on another.\n\nMany internal operations in Meep consist of looping over points in the\n[Yee grid](Yee_Lattice.md), generally performing some operation involving the field\ncomponents and material parameters at each point.\nIn principle, this involves nested `for` loops; in practice,\nit is complicated by several factors, including the following:\n\n+ For calculations that [exploit symmetry](Exploiting_Symmetry.md), only a\nportion of the full grid is actually stored in memory, and obtaining values\nfor field components at a point that *isn't* stored requires a tricky\nprocedure discussed below.\n\n+ Similarly, for Bloch-periodic geometries, only grid points in the unit cell\nare stored, but we may want the fields at a point lying outside the unit cell,\nagain requiring a bit of a shell game to process correctly.\n\n+ Because of the staggered nature of the [Yee grid](Yee_Lattice.md),\n\"looping over grid points\" can mean multiple things &mdash; are we visiting\nonly **E**-field sites, or only **H**-field sites, or both? Either\nway, obtaining a full set of field-component values at any one grid point\nnecessarily involves a certain average over neighboring grid points.\n\nTo shield developers from the need to grapple with these complications\nwhen implementing loops over grid points, `libmeep` provides\na convenient routine called `loop_in_chunks` and a set of macros\nthat take care of many of the above hassles. This is discussed in more\ndetail below.\n\n[TOC]\n\n## Chunk Data Structures\n\nFor each chunk in a geometry, `libmeep` creates instances of\nthe data structures `structure_chunk` (storing data on the\ngeometry of the chunk and the material properties at grid\npoints in the chunk) and `fields_chunk` (storing the actual values\nof the time-domain field components at grid points in the chunk).\nFrequency-domain (DFT) field components are handled by a separate\ndata structure called `dft_chunk.` Each instance of `dft_chunk`\nis associated with a single instance of `fields_chunk` (namely,\nwhichever one stores the time-domain fields at the grid points\ncovered by the DFT chunk); however, because DFT fields are typically\nonly tabulated on a subset of the full grid, the grid volume\ncovered by a `dft_chunk` may be only a subset of the volume\ncovered by its parent `fields_chunk`, and not all `fields_chunks`\nhave `dft_chunks` associated with them.\n\n## Chunking of a 2d Geometry\n\nOur running example throughout this page will be a 2d geometry,\nof dimensions $(L_x, L_y)=(8,6)$, with PML layers of thickness 1\non all sides, discretized with 5 points per unit length\nto yield a 40 &times; 30 grid.\n\n### Chunking in the Single-Processor Case\n\nIn a single-processor run, `libmeep` subdivides this geometry\ninto 9 chunks (click for larger image):\n\n<p align=\"center\"> <a href=\"../images/Chunks_NP1.png\"><img src=\"../images/Chunks_NP1.png\" style='height: 100%; width: 100%; object-fit: contain'/></a></p>\n\nThe width of the 8 chunks around the perimeter is set by the PML thickness.\n\nNote that the chunks are not of uniform sizes and that their ordering is somewhat arbitrary. In particular, consecutive chunks are *not* necessarily adjacent.\n\n#### Chunk Statistics\n\nAs noted above, each chunk is a contiguous region of space defined\nby a Cartesian product of intervals for each coordinate; to specify\nthe extents of the chunk it thus suffices to specify the endpoints\nof the interval for each coordinate, or equivalently the coordinates\nof the lower-left and upper-right grid points in the chunk. For each\nchunk, these are represented by `ivecs` named `is` and `ie`\n(stored in the `fields_chunk` and `dft_chunk` structures).\n\nHere's an example of how this looks for chunk 3 in the figure above:\n\n<p align=\"center\"> <a href=\"../images/ChunkStatistics.png\"><img src=\"../images/ChunkStatistics.png\" style='height: 100%; width: 100%; object-fit: contain'/></a></p>\n\nIn this case we have `is=(29,-29)` and `ie=(39,-19)`.\n\n### Chunking in the Multiprocessor Case\n\nWhen running in parallel mode, each of the chunks identified for the\nsingle-processor case may be further subdivided into new chunks which\ncan be assigned to different processors.\nFor example, on a run with 8 processors, the 9 chunks identified\nin the single-processor case become 24 chunks:\n\n<p align=\"center\"> <a href=\"../images/Chunks_NP8.png\"><img src=\"../images/Chunks_NP8.png\" style='height: 100%; width: 100%; object-fit: contain'/></a></p>\n\nIn this image, grid points with different $z$ coordinates (different\nheights off the $xy$ plane) are handled by different processors,\nwhile points with the same $z$ coordinate but different colors\nlive in different chunks. In this case, processes 0, 2, 5, and 7\neach own 4 chunks, while processes 1, 3, 4, and 6 each own 2 chunks.\n\n## Symmetries\n\nMeep's approach to handling symmetries is discussed\nfrom the user's perspective in [Exploiting Symmetry](Exploiting_Symmetry.md)\nand from a high-level algorithmic perspective in [Computer Physics Communications, Vol. 181, pp. 687-702 (2010)](http://ab-initio.mit.edu/~oskooi/papers/Oskooi10.pdf).\n\nThe following is a brief synopsis of the implementation of this feature.\n\n+ The action of the symmetry group classifies grid points into *orbits,*\n  sets of grid points that transform into one another under symmetry\n  transformations. For example, in the figure with XY mirror symmetry below,\n  the orbit of\n  $\\mathbf{x}_a$ is $\\{\\mathbf{x}_a, \\mathbf{x}_b, \\mathbf{x}_c, \\mathbf{x}_d\\}$.\n  Meep chooses one element from each orbit (the \"parent\" grid point)\n  to serve as a representative of the orbit, with the remaining elements of\n  the orbit classified as \"children\" equivalent to the parent under\n  the group action.\n  (Any point in the orbit could serve equally well as the parent;\n   the convention in meep is to choose the point with the lowest (most negative)\n   grid indices, i.e the point closest to the lower-left corner of the overall\n   grid---$\\mathbf{x}_a$ in this case---but nothing depends on this particular choice.)\n\n+ For each orbit, field components are only stored for the parent, not for\n  any children. This reduces memory requirements by a factor $M$,\n  the number of points in each orbit, known in meep as the ``multiplicity''\n  of the symmetry; for example, $M=2$ for a geometry with *Y*-mirror symmetry,\n  $M=4$ for an *XY*-mirror symmetry, $M=N$ for an *N*-fold rotational\n  symmetry, etc.\n\n+ Loops over grid points run only over parent points, i.e. points with field\n  components stored in memory. However, each parent point is now visited\n  $M$ times, once for each distinct symmetry transformation\n  $\\mathcal{S}_m (m=1,\\cdots,M) $ in the symmetry group\n  (including the identity transformation). On the $m$th visit to a given\n  parent point $\\mathbf{x}_p$, we\n\n    **(1)** look up the components of the fields $\\mathbf{E}_p, \\mathbf{H}_p$\n            stored in memory for $\\mathbf{x}_p$,\n\n    **(2)** apply the transformation $\\mathcal{S}_m$ to both the grid-point\n            coordinates and the field components of the parent point to yield\n            the coordinates and field components of the $m$th child point, i.e.\n            $$       \\mathbf{x}_{cm} = \\mathcal{S}_m \\mathbf{x}_p,\n              \\quad \\mathbf{E}_{cm} = \\mathcal{S}_m \\mathbf{E}_p,\n              \\quad \\mathbf{H}_{cm} = \\mathcal{S}_m \\mathbf{H}_p.\n            $$\n           If the materials are anisotropic (i.e. the permittivity and/or permeability\n           are tensors) we must transform those appropriately as well.\n\n    **(3)** use the coordinates and field components of the child point to carry\n            out the operation in question.\n\n### Chunking in the Presence of Symmetries\n\nAs noted above, in the presence of symmetries only a portion of the\nfull grid is actually stored in memory. For example, adding a $y$ mirror\nsymmetry (symmetry under reflection about the $x$-axis) eliminates\npoints in the upper half-plane $(y>0)$; the points that remain are\nnow subdivided into 6 chunks (in the single-processor case):\n\n<p align=\"center\"> <a href=\"../images/Chunks_YSymmetry.png\"><img src=\"../images/Chunks_YSymmetry.png\" style='height: 100%; width: 100%; object-fit: contain'/></a></p>\n\nAdding an $x$ mirror symmetry on top of this (so that now the geometry has\nboth $x$ and $y$ mirror symmetry) reduces the number of stored grid points by an\nadditional factor of 2; now the geometry is subdivided into just 4 chunks\nin the single-processor case:\n\n<p align=\"center\"> <a href=\"../images/Chunks_XYSymmetry.png\"><img src=\"../images/Chunks_XYSymmetry.png\" style='height: 100%; width: 100%; object-fit: contain'/></a></p>\n\nIn these figures, points in shaded regions are \"children\" &mdash; that is, points\nfor which Meep stores no field components, since they are related by symmetry\nto \"parent\" points in the unshaded region. In the second figure we have\nindicated one complete orbit: parent point $\\mathbf{x}_a$ is carried to\nchild points $\\{\\mathbf{x}_b, \\mathbf{x}_c, \\mathbf{x}_d\\}$ under the\noperations of the symmetry group.\n\n### Coordinates and Field Components of Symmetry-Reduced Points\n\nSymmetry transformations in `libmeep` are described by a class called\nsimply `symmetry,` which offers class methods for transforming grid\npoints and field components:\n\n```c++\n\n  symmetry S = mirror(X,gv) + mirror(Y,gv);    // XY mirror symmetry\n\n  ivec iparent;                                // grid indices of parent point\n  vec  rparent;                                // cartesian coordinates of parent point\n\n  ...\n\n  ivec ichild = S.transform(iparent, +1);      // grid indices of child point\n   vec rchild = S.transform(rparent, +1);      // cartesian coordinates of child point\n\n  component cchild  = Ex;                      // desired field component at child point\n  component cparent = S.transform(cchild, -1); // corresponding component at parent point\n```\n\n## The `loop_in_chunks` Routine\n\nTo allow developers to implement loops over grid points without\nstressing out over the various complications outlined above,\nthe `fields` class in `libmeep` offers a convenient method called\n`loop_in_chunks.`\n\nTo use this routine, you will first write a \"chunk-loop function\"\nwhich carries out some operation involving grid points and (optionally)\nfield components at grid points. Then you pass your routine to\n`loop_in_chunks` with some additional arguments customizing the\ntype of loop you want (see below). Your loop function will then be\ncalled once for every `chunk` in the problem---including both\nchunks whose fields are present in memory, and those\nwhose aren't due to being eliminated by symmetry---with a long list\nof arguments describing the chunk in question.\n\nThe body of your chunk-loop function will typically want to execute\na loop over all grid points in the chunk. This is facilitated by a host\nof utility macros and API functions that operate on the arguments to your function\nto yield quantities of interest: grid-point coordinates, field-component\nvalues, etc.\n\n### The Chunk Loop Function\n\nThe chunk-loop function that you write and pass to `loop_in_chunks`\nhas the following prototype:\n\n```c++\nvoid field_chunkloop(fields_chunk *fc, int ichunk, component cgrid, ivec is, ivec ie,\n                     vec s0, vec s1, vec e0, vec e1, double dV0, double dV1,\n                     ivec shift, std::complex<double> shift_phase,\n\t             const symmetry &S, int sn, void *chunkloop_data);\n```\n\nNotwithstanding this formidable-looking beast of a calling convention,\nmost of the arguments here are things that you can blindly pass on to\nAPI functions and convenience macros, which will return quantities whose\nsignificance is easy to understand.\n\nHere's a skeleton chunk-loop function\nthat executes a loop over all grid points in the chunk,\nobtaining on each loop iteration both the integer indices and the cartesian\ncoordinates of the child point, as well as values for a list\nof field components of interest (specified before the loop in the\nconstructor of `chunkloop_field_components`). You can fill in the rest of the loop body\nto do whatever you want with `ichild,` `rchild,` and `data.values,` and the\nresults will be identical whether or not you declare symmetries when\ndefining your geometry. (Well, the results will be identical assuming\nthe physical problem you're considering really is symmetric, which Meep [does not check](Exploiting_Symmetry.md).)\n\n```c++\nvoid my_chunkloop(fields_chunk *fc, int ichunk, component cgrid, ivec is, ivec ie,\n                  vec s0, vec s1, vec e0, vec e1, double dV0, double dV1,\n                  ivec shift, std::complex<double> shift_phase,\n\t          const symmetry &S, int sn, void *chunkloop_data)\n{\n  // some preliminary setup\n  vec rshift(shift * (0.5*fc->gv.inva));  // shift into unit cell for PBC geometries\n\n  // prepare the list of field components to fetch at each grid point\n  component components[] = {Ex, Hz};\n  chunkloop_field_components data(fc, cgrid, shift_phase, S, sn, 2, components);\n\n  // loop over all grid points in chunk\n  LOOP_OVER_IVECS(fc->gv, is, ie, idx)\n   {\n     // get grid indices and coordinates of parent point\n     IVEC_LOOP_ILOC(gv, iparent);  // grid indices\n     IVEC_LOOP_LOC(gv, rparent);   // cartesian coordinates\n\n     // apply symmetry transform to get grid indices and coordinates of child point\n     ivec ichild = S.transform(iparent, sn) + shift;\n     vec rchild = S.transform(rparent, sn) + rshift;\n\n     // fetch field components at child point\n     data.update_values(idx);\n     std::complex<double> Ex = data.values[0],\n                          Hz = data.values[1];\n   }\n}\n```\n\n## Is There a Version of `loop_in_chunks` for `dft_chunks`?\n\nNo, but the routine `process_dft_component()` in `src/dft.cpp` effectively\nimplements such a routine for a hard-coded set of operations on DFT\ncomponents (namely: outputting to HDF5, fetching DFT array slices,\nand computing mode-overlap coefficients).\n\n## How the Images were Created\n\nThe images above were obtained with the help of a simple C++ code\ncalled `WriteChunkInfo` that calls `libmeep` API functions to\nobtain info on the chunk structure of the 40&times;30 grid\nwe considered. This code (plus a simple hand-written `Makefile`)\nlives in the `doc/docs/Developer_Codes` subdirectory of the meep source\ndistribution.\n\n+ [`WriteChunkInfo.cpp`](/Developer_Codes/WriteChunkInfo.cpp)\n+ [`Makefile.manual`](/Developer_Codes/Makefile.manual)\n","numLines":303,"startLine":1,"totalLines":303}}}
{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_function_q89vxkrvfb7g_2","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t---\n2\t# Parallel Meep\n3\t---\n4\t\n5\tMeep supports [distributed-memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_memory) parallelism via [MPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Message_Passing_Interface). This allows it to scale up from single multi-core machines to multi-node [clusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_cluster) and [supercomputers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercomputer), and to work on large problems that may not fit into the memory of one machine. Meep simulations can use hundreds of processors, if necessary. Of course, your problem must be sufficiently large in order to [benefit from many processors](FAQ.md#should-i-expect-linear-speedup-from-the-parallel-meep). (Note that it is *not* possible to run a parallel simulation from within a notebook environment.)  Note also that you should not generally use more MPI processes than you have [physical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyper-threading) cores.\n6\t\n7\t[TOC]\n8\t\n9\tInstalling Parallel Meep\n10\t------------------------\n11\t\n12\tTo build from source the parallel version of Meep, you must have a version of MPI installed on your system. For an overview, see [Build From Source/MPI](Build_From_Source.md#mpi).\n13\t\n14\tWe also strongly recommend installing the [HDF5 package](Build_From_Source.md#hdf5) with **parallel** I/O support if you are going to run with more than a few cores/processors. When building from source, HDF5 needs to be configured with the flag `--enable-parallel`. You may also have to set the `CC` environment variable to `mpicc`.\n15\t\n16\tIf you don't install HDF5 with parallel I/O support, you can still do I/O from MPI &mdash; Meep has some hacks to let it write HDF5 files using serial I/O from multiple processes, one at a time. However, this does not scale very well to many processors. Some MPI implementations have been observed to freeze under the strain of trying to write from many processes at once.\n17\t\n18\tThen you just configure Meep with the flag `--with-mpi`. If you run the resulting Python or Scheme script, it runs on a single process; to run with multiple cores/processors you should use `mpirun` as described in the next section. Because you can run the parallel Meep in a single process using this approach (i.e., `mpirun -np 1 python foo.py` or just `python foo.py`, `mpirun -np 1 meep foo.ctl` or just `meep foo.ctl`), there is no need to separately compile and install the serial version of Meep.\n19\t\n20\tUsing Parallel Meep\n21\t-------------------\n22\t\n23\tThe parallel version of Meep is designed to operate completely transparently: you use the **same** Python or Scheme script as for the serial version; the output is the same but it is just faster. In Python, the output of each process that is not the master (rank 0) is sent to [`devnull`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Null_device), and in Scheme, the special `print` function only prints output from the master process.\n24\t\n25\tIn order to run MPI programs, you typically have to use a command like `mpirun` with an argument to indicate how many processes you want to use. Consult your MPI documentation. For example, with many popular MPI implementations, to run with 4 processes you would use something like:\n26\t\n27\t**Python**\n28\t```sh\n29\tmpirun -np 4 python foo.py > foo.out\n30\t```\n31\t\n32\t**Scheme**\n33\t```sh\n34\tmpirun -np 4 meep foo.ctl > foo.out\n35\t```\n36\t\n37\tThere is one important requirement: every MPI process must be able to read the `foo.py`/`foo.ctl` input file or whatever your script file is called. On most systems, this is no problem, but if for some reason your MPI processes don't all have access to the local filesystem then you may need to make copies of your input file or something. This requirement also applies to HDF5 files used for input (i.e., via `epsilon_input_file`) or output (i.e., `output_epsilon()`, `output_efield()`, etc.). Any disruptions to the network or disk failures on individual machines which affect the [network file system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_File_System) may cause Meep to freeze/hang.\n38\t\n39\tFor a potential improvement in [load balancing](FAQ.md#should-i-expect-linear-speedup-from-the-parallel-meep), you can try setting [`split_chunks_evenly=False`](Python_User_Interface.md#the-simulation-class) in the `Simulation` constructor. For a technical description of the load-balancing features in Meep as well as some performance metrics from actual experiments, see [arXiv:2003.04287](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.04287).\n40\t\n41\tIn general, you cannot run Meep interactively on multiple processors.\n42\t\n43\t**Warning:** when running a parallel PyMeep job, the failure of any one MPI process may cause the simulation to deadlock and not abort. This is due to a [behavior of `mpi4py`](https://mpi4py.readthedocs.io/en/stable/mpi4py.run.html). To avoid having to manually kill all the remaining processes, a simple solution is to load the `mpi4py` module (for versions 3.0+) on the `mpirun` command line:\n44\t```sh\n45\tmpirun -np 4 python -m mpi4py foo.py\n46\t```\n47\t\n48\t### Different Forms of Parallelization\n49\t\n50\tParallel Meep works by taking your simulation and dividing the cell among the MPI processes. This is the only way of parallelizing a single simulation and enables simulating very large problems.\n51\t\n52\tHowever, there is an alternative strategy for parallelization. If you have many smaller simulations that you want to run, say for many different values of some parameter, then you can just run these as separate jobs. Such parallelization is known as [embarrassingly parallel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embarrassingly_parallel) because no communication is required. Additionally, Meep provides explicit support for this mode of operation even when using a *single* MPI job via the `meep.divide_parallel_processes(N)` routine which divides `N` MPI processes into `N` equal subgroups and returns the index `n` (`0`,...,`N-1`) of the current group which can be used to decide which simulation to run. That is, you have one script, and the script only creates *one* `Simulation` object — depending on the value of `n` that it receives, it will create a different `Simulation` object (i.e., using different parameters). For each subgroup, Meep acts as though it were running a separate self-contained parallel simulation: the fields from a given subgroup communicate only with each other using MPI, and each subgroup has its own master process with rank 0 which can be checked using `meep.am_master()`.    The overall master process of the entire run is the one for which `meep.am_really_master()` returns `True`; this is the only process that can generally perform I/O.  There is an auxiliary routine `meep.merge_subgroup_data(data)` which takes a NumPy array `data` from every process (which is identical across each subgroup) and then returns an array which is just the concatenated `data` from each subgroup. For an example, see [python/tests/divide_mpi_processes.py](https://github.com/NanoComp/meep/tree/master/python/tests/divide_mpi_processes.py) in the source repository.  You can also communicate between subgroups in other ways, e.g. by using low-level `mpi4py` functions.\n53\t\n54\tThe `divide_parallel_processes` feature can be useful for large supercomputers which typically restrict the total number of jobs that can be executed but do not restrict the size of each job, or for large-scale optimization where many separate simulations are coupled by an optimization algorithm. Note that when using this feature using the [Python interface](Python_User_Interface.md), only the output of the subgroup belonging to the master process of the entire simulation is shown in the standard output. (In C++, the master process from *every* subgroup prints to standard output.)\n55\t\n56\tMeep also supports [thread-level parallelism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Task_parallelism) (i.e., multi-threading) on a single, shared-memory, multi-core machine for the fields updates during timestepping as well as multi-frequency [near-to-far field](Python_User_Interface.md#near-to-far-field-spectra) computations. To use this feature, you will need to [compile Meep from source](Build_From_Source.md#meep) using the `--with-openmp` flag and set the environment variable `OMP_NUM_THREADS` at runtime via e.g., `$ env OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 mpirun -np 2 python foo.py`.\n57\t\n58\t### Optimization Studies of Parallel Simulations\n59\t\n60\tWhen running Meep simulations as part of an optimization study (e.g., via the [adjoint solver](Python_Tutorials/Adjoint_Solver.md)), in order to keep all processes synchronized *every* process runs the same optimization algorithm on the same optimization variables. The overhead of duplicating the computational cost of the optimization algorithm and storage of the design variables across all processes is negligible compared to those of the Meep simulation.\n61\t\n62\tFor comparison, consider the scenario where the optimization runs on just a single master process. That would mean that during each iteration of the optimization after the Meep simulation has computed the objective function (and its gradient), only the master process uses this information to update the optimization parameters (i.e., the design region). The master process would then need to send the updated design region to the other processes so that they could all begin the next Meep simulation. As a result, additional bookkeeping is required to synchronize the processes.\n63\t\n64\tNote: for optimization studies involving *random* initial conditions, the seed of the random number generator must be specified otherwise each process will have a different initial condition which will cause a crash. For example, if you are initializing the design variables with `numpy.random.rand`, then you should call `numpy.random.seed(...)` to set the same `numpy.random` seed on every process.\n65\t\n66\t### User-Specified Cell Partition\n67\t\n68\tAn alternative to having Meep automatically partition the cell at runtime into chunks based on the number of MPI processes is to manually specify the cell partition via the `chunk_layout` parameter of the `Simulation` constructor as a [`BinaryPartition`](Python_User_Interface.md#binarypartition) class object. This is based on representing an arbitrary cell partition as a [binary tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_tree) for which the nodes define \"cuts\" at a given point (e.g., -4.5, 6.3) along a given cell direction and the leaves define an integer-valued process ID (equivalent to the rank of the MPI process for that chunk). Note also that the same process ID can be assigned to as many chunks as you want, which just means that one process timesteps multiple chunks. If you use fewer MPI processes, then the process ID is taken modulo the number of MPI processes. If you use more MPI processes than there are chunks, then those MPI processes that are not assigned to chunks will just remain idle. Finally, any absorbing boundary layers (i.e., PMLs) surrounding the cell will automatically be defined as separate chunks and assigned the same process ID as the original chunk from which they were split off from.\n69\t\n70\tAs a demonstration, an example of a 2d cell partition along with its binary-tree representation is shown below. The 10×5 cell in $xy$ coordinates with origin at the cell center is partitioned into five chunks numbered one through five.\n71\t\n72\t\n73\t![](images/chunk_division_binary_tree.png#center)\n74\t\n75\t\n76\tThis binary tree can be described as a list of lists where each list entry is `[ (split_dir,split_pos), left, right ]` for which `split_dir` and `split_pos` define the splitting direction and position, and `left` and `right` are the left and right branches which can be either another list defining a new node or a process ID. Based on these specifications, the cell partition from above can be set up as follows:\n77\t\n78\t```py\n79\timport meep as mp\n80\timport matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n81\t\n82\tchunk_layout = mp.BinaryPartition(data=[ (mp.X,-2.0), 0, [ (mp.Y,1.5),\n83\t                                         [ (mp.X,3.0), 1, [ (mp.Y,-0.5), 4, 3 ] ], 2 ] ])\n84\t\n85\tcell_size = mp.Vector3(10.0,5.0,0)\n86\t\n87\tsim = mp.Simulation(cell_size=cell_size,\n88\t                    resolution=10,\n89\t                    chunk_layout=chunk_layout)\n90\t\n91\tsim.visualize_chunks()\n92\tplt.savefig('chunk_layout.png',dpi=150,bbox_inches='tight')\n93\t```\n94\t\n95\tFor improved performance, we recommend ordering the process IDs in [depth-first order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth-first_search) of the tree, which will tend to give spatially adjacent chunks nearby process IDs.  This increases the chance that adjacent chunks are on the same MPI node, improving communication speeds.\n96\t\n97\tTechnical Details\n98\t-----------------\n99\t\n100\tWhen you run Meep under MPI, the following is a brief description of what is happening behind the scenes. For the most part, you shouldn't need to know this stuff. Just use the same Python/Scheme script file exactly as you would for a uniprocessor simulation.\n101\t\n102\tFirst, every MPI process executes the Python/Scheme file in parallel. The processes communicate however, to only perform one simulation in sync with one another. In particular, the cell is divided into \"chunks,\" one per process, to roughly equally divide the work and the memory. For additional details, see [Chunks and Symmetry](Chunks_and_Symmetry.md) as well as Section 2.2 (\"Grid chunks and owned points\") of [Computer Physics Communications, Vol. 181, pp. 687-702 (2010)](http://ab-initio.mit.edu/~oskooi/papers/Oskooi10.pdf).\n103\t\n104\tWhen you time-step via Python's `meep.Simulation.run(until=...)` or Scheme's `run-until`, etc., the chunks are time-stepped in parallel, communicating the values of the pixels on their boundaries with one another. In general, any Meep function that performs some collective operation over the whole cell or a large portion thereof is parallelized, including: time-stepping, HDF5 I/O, accumulation of flux spectra, and field integration via `integrate_field_function` (Python) or `integrate-field-function` (Scheme), although the *results* are communicated to all processes.\n105\t\n106\tComputations that only involve isolated points, such as `get_field_point` (Python) or `get-field-point` (Scheme), or `Harminv` (Python) or `harminv` (Scheme) analyses, are performed by all processes redundantly. In the case of `get_field_point` or `get-field-point`, Meep figures out which process \"knows\" the field at the given field, and then sends the field value from that process to all other processes. This is harmless because such computations are rarely performance bottlenecks.\n107\t\n108\tAlthough all processes execute the Python/Scheme file in parallel, print statements are ignored for all process but one (process \\#0). In this way, you only get one copy of the output.\n109\t\n110\tSometimes you only want an operation to take place on one process. A common use case is showing a `matplotlib` plot with `plt.show()`, or saving a file with `plt.savefig()`. In cases where you need to distinguish different MPI processes in your Python/Scheme file, you can use the following functions:\n111\t\n112\t**`meep.am_master()`**,\n113\t**`(meep-am-master)`**\n114\t—\n115\tReturns true if the current process is the master process (rank 0).\n116\t\n117\tThis can be useful for calling external I/O or visualization routines, e.g. Matplotlib plotting functions, that you only want to execute on the master process.   Note that the Scheme `(print)` or Python `print` functions are *already* set up so that by default their output is suppressed on non-master processes.\n118\t\n119\t**Warning**: Most Meep functions operating on the simulation (e.g. fields or structure) are \"collective\" operations that must be called from all processes in the same sequence — if you call them from only one process via `am_master` (or `my_rank`) checks, then they will [deadlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadlock).  Code inside an `am_master` check should generally only call non-Meep library functions.\n120\t\n121\t**`meep.count_processors()`**,\n122\t**`(meep-count-processors)`**\n123\t—\n124\tReturns the number of processes that Meep is using in parallel.\n125\t\n126\t**`meep.my_rank()`**,\n127\t**`(meep-my-rank)`**\n128\t—\n129\tReturns the index of the process running the current file, from zero to `meep.count_processors()`-1.\n130\t\n131\t**`meep.all_wait()`**,\n132\t**`(meep-all-wait)`**\n133\t—\n134\tBlocks until all processes execute this statement (MPI_Barrier).\n135\t\n136\tFor large multicore jobs with I/O, it may be necessary to have `(meep-all-wait)` as the last line in the Scheme file to ensure that all processors terminate at the same point in the execution. Otherwise, one processor may finish and abruptly terminate the other processors.\n137\t\n138\tRuntime Scaling on MPI Clusters\n139\t-------------------------------\n140\t\n141\tThe following are benchmarking results of the total runtime vs. number of processors for a 3d [OLED](http://www.simpetus.com/projects.html#meep_oled) simulation involving [Lorentzian susceptibility](Python_User_Interface.md#lorentziansusceptibility), [Absorber](Python_User_Interface.md#absorber), 1d [PML](Python_User_Interface.md#pml), and [DFT flux monitors](Python_User_Interface.md#flux-spectra) for [MPICH](https://www.mpich.org/) clusters of [n1-standard-16](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/machine-types#n1_machine_type) instances (8 single-threaded cores) on the [Google Cloud Platform](https://cloud.google.com/) (GCP). One slot on each node is reserved for kernel tasks leaving 7 slots per node. The software stack includes Ubuntu 16.04, the Meep 1.15 [Conda package](Installation.md#conda-packages), [elasticluster](https://elasticluster.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) for the cluster management, and [grid engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oracle_Grid_Engine) for the job scheduler. In order to reduce [cache contention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resource_contention), process affinity is used via the `mpirun` option `-bind-to core`. Meep's simulation domain is split into equal-sized [chunks](Chunks_and_Symmetry.md#chunks-and-symmetry) (`split_chunks_evenly=True`). There are 13 clusters ranging in size from 2 to 14 nodes (14 to 98 processors). For reference, there are some [useful guidelines for benchmarking MPI jobs](https://www.open-mpi.org/faq/?category=tuning#running-perf-numbers).\n142\t\n143\tAs shown in the first figure below, the runtime reaches a minimum at 77 processors. The second figure shows the scaling of the ratio of the mean time spent on communication (MPI/synchronization) to the computation (time stepping and DFTs). (Timing metrics were obtained using [`Simulation.mean_time_spent_on`](Python_User_Interface.md#simulation-time).) This ratio is a measure of the parallelization efficiency. The crossover point when the parallelization efficiency becomes larger than one — the regime in which the simulation is constrained by the network bandwidth rather than the CPU clock speed — corresponds well to the minimum runtime of the first figure.\n144\t\n145\t\n146\t![](images/parallel_benchmark_runtime_vs_nprocs.png#center)\n147\t\n148\t\n149\t\n150\t![](images/parallel_benchmark_commcomp_vs_nprocs.png#center)\n151\t\n152\t\n153\tThese results are not continuous because as the number of processors changes slightly (e.g., from 42 to 49), the chunk divisions can change by a lot (i.e., it can switch from splitting some chunk along the $x$ axis to along the $y$ axis) which significantly affects the runtime performance. Also, in general, benchmarking studies involving MPI jobs are challenging because there are [a number of factors which can affect the results](https://www.open-mpi.org/faq/?category=tuning#running-perf-numbers).\n154\t\n155\tFor a given cluster, we can also analyze the time spent by each processor on time-stepping, MPI/synchronization, and DFT. This is shown in the next figure for the case of a cluster with 35 processors (5 nodes). Because the simulation is not properly load balanced due to the equal-sized chunks, there is a large variation in the timings for different processors particularly for the DFT where there are several idle processors (i.e., chunks which do not contain any DFT pixels).\n156\t\n157\t\n158\t![](images/parallel_benchmark_barplot.png#center)\n159\t\n160\t\n161\tBased on these results, we plot the average of the *inverse* of the timings (proportional to the number of cycles per second; a \"rate\" quantity which can demonstrate linear scaling) for the time-stepping and DFT over the full range of cluster sizes. The time-stepping results demonstrate (approximately) linear scaling.  The size of the error bars increases with the number of cluster nodes mainly due to pronounced variations in the network bandwidth; the N1 instances do *not* support colocation via a [compact placement policy](https://cloud.google.com/solutions/best-practices-for-using-mpi-on-compute-engine). The DFT results (which excludes those processors without any DFT pixels) seem to be oscillating around a constant. This is not surprising because the processor(s) which takes the longest time to update its DFT pixels sets an upper bound on how fast the DFT calculation for all processors can proceed. It is the presence of this unique upper bound for each cluster which is revealed by the scaling plot.\n162\t\n163\tSee also [FAQ/Should I expect linear speedup from the parallel Meep](FAQ.md#should-i-expect-linear-speedup-from-the-parallel-meep)?\n164\t\n165\t\n166\t![](images/parallel_benchmark_timestep.png#center)\n167\t\n168\t\n169\t\n170\t![](images/parallel_benchmark_DFT.png#center)\n171\t\n172\t\n173\t\n174\tDynamic Chunk Balancing\n175\t-----------------------\n176\t\n177\tSince Meep's computation time is ultimately bottlenecked by the slowest-running process, it is desirable to load-balance the chunk layout such that each compute node is given an equal workload. By default, Meep uses a heuristics-based scheme to estimate the cost of a computation region based on the composition of voxel types (anisotropic, PML, etc.) However, this method of estimating the simulation time for a chunk in advance is not always accurate, a problem which is especially true for simulations run on shared-resource clusters. Meep's `chunk_balancer` module allows for a more empirical, data-driven approach for dynamically load-balancing parallel simulations. This approach uses the simulation time per node to adaptively modify the chunk layout and it implicitly corrects for heterogeneity over the simulation region and variability in background loads and job priority on shared compute resources. This approach can be especially useful for cases such as adjoint optimization, where slight variations on the same simulation are run many times over many iterations.\n178\t\n179\t\n180\t![](images/adaptive_chunk_layout.gif#center)\n181\t\n182\t\n183\t### Chunk balancer interface\n184\t\n185\tThe chunk balancer interface provides four main methods:\n186\t- `make_initial_chunk_layout()` generates the initial chunk layout for the first iteration of a simulation. By default, `None` is returned, indicating Meep should use its default chunk partitioning strategy.\n187\t- `should_adjust_chunk_layout()` decides whether the current layout is sufficiently poorly balanced to justify the up-front cost of reallocating the field arrays when changing chunk layouts.\n188\t- `compute_new_chunk_layout()` looks at the current chunk layout and per-process timing data to compute a new chunk layout which has chunk sizes adjusted to improve the load balance across compute nodes.\n189\t- `adjust_chunk_layout()` is syntactic sugar which will compute a new chunk layout, apply it to the simulation object, reset the simulation, and re-initialize the simulation.\n190\t\n191\t```py\n192\tclass AbstractChunkBalancer(abc.ABC):\n193\t  \"\"\"Chunk balancer for dynamically load-balanced chunk layouts.\"\"\"\n194\t\n195\t  def make_initial_chunk_layout(self, sim) -> mp.BinaryPartition:\n196\t    \"\"\"Generates an initial chunk layout for simulation.\"\"\"\n197\t\n198\t  def should_adjust_chunk_layout(self, sim) -> bool:\n199\t    \"\"\"Is current layout imbalanced enough to justify rebuilding sim?\"\"\"\n200\t\n201\t  @abc.abstractmethod\n202\t  def compute_new_chunk_layout(\n203\t    self,\n204\t    timing_measurements: MeepTimingMeasurements,\n205\t    old_chunk_layout: mp.BinaryPartition,\n206\t    chunk_volumes: Tuple[mp.grid_volume],\n207\t    chunk_owners: np.ndarray) -> mp.BinaryPartition:\n208\t    \"\"\"Rebalance chunks to equalize simulation time for each node.\"\"\"\n209\t\n210\t  def adjust_chunk_layout(self, sim, **kwargs) -> None:\n211\t    \"\"\"Computes a new chunk layout and applies it to sim.\"\"\"\n212\t```\n213\t\n214\t### Usage\n215\t\n216\tUsing the chunk balancer is very straightforward, and it can typically be integrated into existing Meep simulations with only a few lines of code. Here is a simple example:\n217\t\n218\t```py\n219\tfrom meep.chunk_balancer import ChunkBalancer\n220\t\n221\tchunk_balancer = ChunkBalancer()\n222\t\n223\t# Compute an initial chunk layout\n224\tinitial_chunk_layout = chunk_balancer.make_initial_chunk_layout()\n225\t\n226\tsim = mp.Simulation(..., chunk_layout=initial_chunk_layout)\n227\tsim.init_sim()\n228\t\n229\tfor iteration in range(epochs):\n230\t  sim.run(...)\n231\t  # Adjust the chunk layout for the next iteration if needed\n232\t  chunk_balancer.adjust_chunk_layout(sim, sensitivity=0.4)\n233\t```\n234\t\n235\tChunks can also be rebalanced between runs of a program by dumping and loading the chunk layout from a pickled object. For example:\n236\t\n237\t```py\n238\timport meep as mp\n239\tfrom meep.chunk_balancer import ChunkBalancer\n240\tfrom meep.timing_measurements import MeepTimingMeasurements\n241\timport pickle\n242\timport os.path\n243\t\n244\t# Fetch chunk layout from a previous run if it exists\n245\tif os.path.exists(\"path/to/chunk_layout.pkl\"):\n246\t  initial_chunk_layout = pickle.load(open(\"path/to/chunk_layout.pkl\", \"rb\"))\n247\telse:\n248\t  initial_chunk_layout = None\n249\t\n250\tsim = mp.Simulation(..., chunk_layout=initial_chunk_layout)\n251\tsim.init_sim()\n252\tsim.run(...)\n253\t\n254\t# Compute and save chunk layout for next run\n255\ttimings = MeepTimingMeasurements.new_from_simulation(sim)\n256\tchunk_layout = sim.chunk_layout\n257\tchunk_volumes = sim.structure.get_chunk_volumes()\n258\tchunk_owners = sim.structure.get_chunk_owners()\n259\tnext_chunk_layout = ChunkBalancer().compute_new_chunk_layout(\n260\t    timings,\n261\t    chunk_layout,\n262\t    chunk_volumes,\n263\t    chunk_owners,\n264\t    sensitivity=0.4)\n265\t\n266\t# Save chunk layout for next run\n267\twith open(\"path/to/chunk_layout.pkl\", \"wb\") as f:\n268\t    pickle.dump(next_chunk_layout, f)\n269\t```\n270\t\n271\t### Chunk adjustment algorithm\n272\t\n273\tThe default chunk adjustment algorithm recursively traverses the `BinaryPartition` object and resizes the chunk volumes of the left and right children of each node to have an equal per-node simulation time. The new chunk layout has split positions which are a weighted average of the previous iteration's chunk layout and the newly computed layout, and the `sensitivity` parameter adjusts how fast the chunk sizes are adjusted. (`sensitivity=0.0` means no adjustment, `sensitivity=1.0` means an immediate snap to the predicted split positions, and `sensitivity=0.5` is the average of the old and new layouts.) The adjustment algorithm is summarized in pseudocode below:\n274\t\n275\t```\n276\tdef adjust_split_pos(node):\n277\t  for subtree in {node.left, node.right}:\n278\t    V := Σ volume for nodes in subtree\n279\t    t := Σ sim time for nodes in subtree\n280\t    n := number of processes in subtree\n281\t    l := t / n  # average load per process\n282\t\n283\t  Vₗ ↦ Vₗ / lₗ\n284\t  Vᵣ ↦ Vᵣ / lᵣ\n285\t\n286\t  split_pos’ := dₘᵢₙ + (dₘₐₓ - dₘᵢₙ) * (Vₗ) / (Vₗ + Vᵣ)\n287\t\n288\t  # Adjust with sensitivity parameter\n289\t  node.split_pos ↦ s * split_pos’ + (1-s) * node.split_pos\n290\t\n291\t  # Recurse through rest of the tree\n292\t  adjust_split_pos(node.left)\n293\t  adjust_split_pos(node.right)\n294\t```\n295\t\n296\t### Load balancing results on shared clusters\n297\t\n298\tThe following benchmarking results show load-balancing improvements from a parallel run on a shared compute cluster in a datacenter. The per-core working times (blue and orange) start of initially poorly balanced using the default `split_by_cost` scheme, but the load balancing improves over successive iterations.\n299\t\n300\t\n301\t![](images/chunk_balancer_timing_stats.gif#center)\n302\t\n303\t\n304\tUsing the normalized standard deviation in simulation times per iteration as a proxy for load-balancing efficacy, we can see that the load balance improves over a large number of runs with varying numbers of processes:\n305\t\n306\t\n307\t![](images/chunk_balancer_variance.jpg#center)\n308\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"5d8bf8c1-7393-4a9d-a77c-b479c8cf527b","uuid":"225ec8c4-cba2-408e-bcfd-10029e25907f","timestamp":"2026-04-07T08:38:16.100Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/workspace/autofdtd/../meep/doc/docs/Parallel_Meep.md","content":"---\n# Parallel Meep\n---\n\nMeep supports [distributed-memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_memory) parallelism via [MPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Message_Passing_Interface). This allows it to scale up from single multi-core machines to multi-node [clusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_cluster) and [supercomputers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercomputer), and to work on large problems that may not fit into the memory of one machine. Meep simulations can use hundreds of processors, if necessary. Of course, your problem must be sufficiently large in order to [benefit from many processors](FAQ.md#should-i-expect-linear-speedup-from-the-parallel-meep). (Note that it is *not* possible to run a parallel simulation from within a notebook environment.)  Note also that you should not generally use more MPI processes than you have [physical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyper-threading) cores.\n\n[TOC]\n\nInstalling Parallel Meep\n------------------------\n\nTo build from source the parallel version of Meep, you must have a version of MPI installed on your system. For an overview, see [Build From Source/MPI](Build_From_Source.md#mpi).\n\nWe also strongly recommend installing the [HDF5 package](Build_From_Source.md#hdf5) with **parallel** I/O support if you are going to run with more than a few cores/processors. When building from source, HDF5 needs to be configured with the flag `--enable-parallel`. You may also have to set the `CC` environment variable to `mpicc`.\n\nIf you don't install HDF5 with parallel I/O support, you can still do I/O from MPI &mdash; Meep has some hacks to let it write HDF5 files using serial I/O from multiple processes, one at a time. However, this does not scale very well to many processors. Some MPI implementations have been observed to freeze under the strain of trying to write from many processes at once.\n\nThen you just configure Meep with the flag `--with-mpi`. If you run the resulting Python or Scheme script, it runs on a single process; to run with multiple cores/processors you should use `mpirun` as described in the next section. Because you can run the parallel Meep in a single process using this approach (i.e., `mpirun -np 1 python foo.py` or just `python foo.py`, `mpirun -np 1 meep foo.ctl` or just `meep foo.ctl`), there is no need to separately compile and install the serial version of Meep.\n\nUsing Parallel Meep\n-------------------\n\nThe parallel version of Meep is designed to operate completely transparently: you use the **same** Python or Scheme script as for the serial version; the output is the same but it is just faster. In Python, the output of each process that is not the master (rank 0) is sent to [`devnull`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Null_device), and in Scheme, the special `print` function only prints output from the master process.\n\nIn order to run MPI programs, you typically have to use a command like `mpirun` with an argument to indicate how many processes you want to use. Consult your MPI documentation. For example, with many popular MPI implementations, to run with 4 processes you would use something like:\n\n**Python**\n```sh\nmpirun -np 4 python foo.py > foo.out\n```\n\n**Scheme**\n```sh\nmpirun -np 4 meep foo.ctl > foo.out\n```\n\nThere is one important requirement: every MPI process must be able to read the `foo.py`/`foo.ctl` input file or whatever your script file is called. On most systems, this is no problem, but if for some reason your MPI processes don't all have access to the local filesystem then you may need to make copies of your input file or something. This requirement also applies to HDF5 files used for input (i.e., via `epsilon_input_file`) or output (i.e., `output_epsilon()`, `output_efield()`, etc.). Any disruptions to the network or disk failures on individual machines which affect the [network file system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_File_System) may cause Meep to freeze/hang.\n\nFor a potential improvement in [load balancing](FAQ.md#should-i-expect-linear-speedup-from-the-parallel-meep), you can try setting [`split_chunks_evenly=False`](Python_User_Interface.md#the-simulation-class) in the `Simulation` constructor. For a technical description of the load-balancing features in Meep as well as some performance metrics from actual experiments, see [arXiv:2003.04287](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.04287).\n\nIn general, you cannot run Meep interactively on multiple processors.\n\n**Warning:** when running a parallel PyMeep job, the failure of any one MPI process may cause the simulation to deadlock and not abort. This is due to a [behavior of `mpi4py`](https://mpi4py.readthedocs.io/en/stable/mpi4py.run.html). To avoid having to manually kill all the remaining processes, a simple solution is to load the `mpi4py` module (for versions 3.0+) on the `mpirun` command line:\n```sh\nmpirun -np 4 python -m mpi4py foo.py\n```\n\n### Different Forms of Parallelization\n\nParallel Meep works by taking your simulation and dividing the cell among the MPI processes. This is the only way of parallelizing a single simulation and enables simulating very large problems.\n\nHowever, there is an alternative strategy for parallelization. If you have many smaller simulations that you want to run, say for many different values of some parameter, then you can just run these as separate jobs. Such parallelization is known as [embarrassingly parallel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embarrassingly_parallel) because no communication is required. Additionally, Meep provides explicit support for this mode of operation even when using a *single* MPI job via the `meep.divide_parallel_processes(N)` routine which divides `N` MPI processes into `N` equal subgroups and returns the index `n` (`0`,...,`N-1`) of the current group which can be used to decide which simulation to run. That is, you have one script, and the script only creates *one* `Simulation` object — depending on the value of `n` that it receives, it will create a different `Simulation` object (i.e., using different parameters). For each subgroup, Meep acts as though it were running a separate self-contained parallel simulation: the fields from a given subgroup communicate only with each other using MPI, and each subgroup has its own master process with rank 0 which can be checked using `meep.am_master()`.    The overall master process of the entire run is the one for which `meep.am_really_master()` returns `True`; this is the only process that can generally perform I/O.  There is an auxiliary routine `meep.merge_subgroup_data(data)` which takes a NumPy array `data` from every process (which is identical across each subgroup) and then returns an array which is just the concatenated `data` from each subgroup. For an example, see [python/tests/divide_mpi_processes.py](https://github.com/NanoComp/meep/tree/master/python/tests/divide_mpi_processes.py) in the source repository.  You can also communicate between subgroups in other ways, e.g. by using low-level `mpi4py` functions.\n\nThe `divide_parallel_processes` feature can be useful for large supercomputers which typically restrict the total number of jobs that can be executed but do not restrict the size of each job, or for large-scale optimization where many separate simulations are coupled by an optimization algorithm. Note that when using this feature using the [Python interface](Python_User_Interface.md), only the output of the subgroup belonging to the master process of the entire simulation is shown in the standard output. (In C++, the master process from *every* subgroup prints to standard output.)\n\nMeep also supports [thread-level parallelism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Task_parallelism) (i.e., multi-threading) on a single, shared-memory, multi-core machine for the fields updates during timestepping as well as multi-frequency [near-to-far field](Python_User_Interface.md#near-to-far-field-spectra) computations. To use this feature, you will need to [compile Meep from source](Build_From_Source.md#meep) using the `--with-openmp` flag and set the environment variable `OMP_NUM_THREADS` at runtime via e.g., `$ env OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 mpirun -np 2 python foo.py`.\n\n### Optimization Studies of Parallel Simulations\n\nWhen running Meep simulations as part of an optimization study (e.g., via the [adjoint solver](Python_Tutorials/Adjoint_Solver.md)), in order to keep all processes synchronized *every* process runs the same optimization algorithm on the same optimization variables. The overhead of duplicating the computational cost of the optimization algorithm and storage of the design variables across all processes is negligible compared to those of the Meep simulation.\n\nFor comparison, consider the scenario where the optimization runs on just a single master process. That would mean that during each iteration of the optimization after the Meep simulation has computed the objective function (and its gradient), only the master process uses this information to update the optimization parameters (i.e., the design region). The master process would then need to send the updated design region to the other processes so that they could all begin the next Meep simulation. As a result, additional bookkeeping is required to synchronize the processes.\n\nNote: for optimization studies involving *random* initial conditions, the seed of the random number generator must be specified otherwise each process will have a different initial condition which will cause a crash. For example, if you are initializing the design variables with `numpy.random.rand`, then you should call `numpy.random.seed(...)` to set the same `numpy.random` seed on every process.\n\n### User-Specified Cell Partition\n\nAn alternative to having Meep automatically partition the cell at runtime into chunks based on the number of MPI processes is to manually specify the cell partition via the `chunk_layout` parameter of the `Simulation` constructor as a [`BinaryPartition`](Python_User_Interface.md#binarypartition) class object. This is based on representing an arbitrary cell partition as a [binary tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_tree) for which the nodes define \"cuts\" at a given point (e.g., -4.5, 6.3) along a given cell direction and the leaves define an integer-valued process ID (equivalent to the rank of the MPI process for that chunk). Note also that the same process ID can be assigned to as many chunks as you want, which just means that one process timesteps multiple chunks. If you use fewer MPI processes, then the process ID is taken modulo the number of MPI processes. If you use more MPI processes than there are chunks, then those MPI processes that are not assigned to chunks will just remain idle. Finally, any absorbing boundary layers (i.e., PMLs) surrounding the cell will automatically be defined as separate chunks and assigned the same process ID as the original chunk from which they were split off from.\n\nAs a demonstration, an example of a 2d cell partition along with its binary-tree representation is shown below. The 10×5 cell in $xy$ coordinates with origin at the cell center is partitioned into five chunks numbered one through five.\n\n\n![](images/chunk_division_binary_tree.png#center)\n\n\nThis binary tree can be described as a list of lists where each list entry is `[ (split_dir,split_pos), left, right ]` for which `split_dir` and `split_pos` define the splitting direction and position, and `left` and `right` are the left and right branches which can be either another list defining a new node or a process ID. Based on these specifications, the cell partition from above can be set up as follows:\n\n```py\nimport meep as mp\nimport matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n\nchunk_layout = mp.BinaryPartition(data=[ (mp.X,-2.0), 0, [ (mp.Y,1.5),\n                                         [ (mp.X,3.0), 1, [ (mp.Y,-0.5), 4, 3 ] ], 2 ] ])\n\ncell_size = mp.Vector3(10.0,5.0,0)\n\nsim = mp.Simulation(cell_size=cell_size,\n                    resolution=10,\n                    chunk_layout=chunk_layout)\n\nsim.visualize_chunks()\nplt.savefig('chunk_layout.png',dpi=150,bbox_inches='tight')\n```\n\nFor improved performance, we recommend ordering the process IDs in [depth-first order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth-first_search) of the tree, which will tend to give spatially adjacent chunks nearby process IDs.  This increases the chance that adjacent chunks are on the same MPI node, improving communication speeds.\n\nTechnical Details\n-----------------\n\nWhen you run Meep under MPI, the following is a brief description of what is happening behind the scenes. For the most part, you shouldn't need to know this stuff. Just use the same Python/Scheme script file exactly as you would for a uniprocessor simulation.\n\nFirst, every MPI process executes the Python/Scheme file in parallel. The processes communicate however, to only perform one simulation in sync with one another. In particular, the cell is divided into \"chunks,\" one per process, to roughly equally divide the work and the memory. For additional details, see [Chunks and Symmetry](Chunks_and_Symmetry.md) as well as Section 2.2 (\"Grid chunks and owned points\") of [Computer Physics Communications, Vol. 181, pp. 687-702 (2010)](http://ab-initio.mit.edu/~oskooi/papers/Oskooi10.pdf).\n\nWhen you time-step via Python's `meep.Simulation.run(until=...)` or Scheme's `run-until`, etc., the chunks are time-stepped in parallel, communicating the values of the pixels on their boundaries with one another. In general, any Meep function that performs some collective operation over the whole cell or a large portion thereof is parallelized, including: time-stepping, HDF5 I/O, accumulation of flux spectra, and field integration via `integrate_field_function` (Python) or `integrate-field-function` (Scheme), although the *results* are communicated to all processes.\n\nComputations that only involve isolated points, such as `get_field_point` (Python) or `get-field-point` (Scheme), or `Harminv` (Python) or `harminv` (Scheme) analyses, are performed by all processes redundantly. In the case of `get_field_point` or `get-field-point`, Meep figures out which process \"knows\" the field at the given field, and then sends the field value from that process to all other processes. This is harmless because such computations are rarely performance bottlenecks.\n\nAlthough all processes execute the Python/Scheme file in parallel, print statements are ignored for all process but one (process \\#0). In this way, you only get one copy of the output.\n\nSometimes you only want an operation to take place on one process. A common use case is showing a `matplotlib` plot with `plt.show()`, or saving a file with `plt.savefig()`. In cases where you need to distinguish different MPI processes in your Python/Scheme file, you can use the following functions:\n\n**`meep.am_master()`**,\n**`(meep-am-master)`**\n—\nReturns true if the current process is the master process (rank 0).\n\nThis can be useful for calling external I/O or visualization routines, e.g. Matplotlib plotting functions, that you only want to execute on the master process.   Note that the Scheme `(print)` or Python `print` functions are *already* set up so that by default their output is suppressed on non-master processes.\n\n**Warning**: Most Meep functions operating on the simulation (e.g. fields or structure) are \"collective\" operations that must be called from all processes in the same sequence — if you call them from only one process via `am_master` (or `my_rank`) checks, then they will [deadlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadlock).  Code inside an `am_master` check should generally only call non-Meep library functions.\n\n**`meep.count_processors()`**,\n**`(meep-count-processors)`**\n—\nReturns the number of processes that Meep is using in parallel.\n\n**`meep.my_rank()`**,\n**`(meep-my-rank)`**\n—\nReturns the index of the process running the current file, from zero to `meep.count_processors()`-1.\n\n**`meep.all_wait()`**,\n**`(meep-all-wait)`**\n—\nBlocks until all processes execute this statement (MPI_Barrier).\n\nFor large multicore jobs with I/O, it may be necessary to have `(meep-all-wait)` as the last line in the Scheme file to ensure that all processors terminate at the same point in the execution. Otherwise, one processor may finish and abruptly terminate the other processors.\n\nRuntime Scaling on MPI Clusters\n-------------------------------\n\nThe following are benchmarking results of the total runtime vs. number of processors for a 3d [OLED](http://www.simpetus.com/projects.html#meep_oled) simulation involving [Lorentzian susceptibility](Python_User_Interface.md#lorentziansusceptibility), [Absorber](Python_User_Interface.md#absorber), 1d [PML](Python_User_Interface.md#pml), and [DFT flux monitors](Python_User_Interface.md#flux-spectra) for [MPICH](https://www.mpich.org/) clusters of [n1-standard-16](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/machine-types#n1_machine_type) instances (8 single-threaded cores) on the [Google Cloud Platform](https://cloud.google.com/) (GCP). One slot on each node is reserved for kernel tasks leaving 7 slots per node. The software stack includes Ubuntu 16.04, the Meep 1.15 [Conda package](Installation.md#conda-packages), [elasticluster](https://elasticluster.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) for the cluster management, and [grid engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oracle_Grid_Engine) for the job scheduler. In order to reduce [cache contention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resource_contention), process affinity is used via the `mpirun` option `-bind-to core`. Meep's simulation domain is split into equal-sized [chunks](Chunks_and_Symmetry.md#chunks-and-symmetry) (`split_chunks_evenly=True`). There are 13 clusters ranging in size from 2 to 14 nodes (14 to 98 processors). For reference, there are some [useful guidelines for benchmarking MPI jobs](https://www.open-mpi.org/faq/?category=tuning#running-perf-numbers).\n\nAs shown in the first figure below, the runtime reaches a minimum at 77 processors. The second figure shows the scaling of the ratio of the mean time spent on communication (MPI/synchronization) to the computation (time stepping and DFTs). (Timing metrics were obtained using [`Simulation.mean_time_spent_on`](Python_User_Interface.md#simulation-time).) This ratio is a measure of the parallelization efficiency. The crossover point when the parallelization efficiency becomes larger than one — the regime in which the simulation is constrained by the network bandwidth rather than the CPU clock speed — corresponds well to the minimum runtime of the first figure.\n\n\n![](images/parallel_benchmark_runtime_vs_nprocs.png#center)\n\n\n\n![](images/parallel_benchmark_commcomp_vs_nprocs.png#center)\n\n\nThese results are not continuous because as the number of processors changes slightly (e.g., from 42 to 49), the chunk divisions can change by a lot (i.e., it can switch from splitting some chunk along the $x$ axis to along the $y$ axis) which significantly affects the runtime performance. Also, in general, benchmarking studies involving MPI jobs are challenging because there are [a number of factors which can affect the results](https://www.open-mpi.org/faq/?category=tuning#running-perf-numbers).\n\nFor a given cluster, we can also analyze the time spent by each processor on time-stepping, MPI/synchronization, and DFT. This is shown in the next figure for the case of a cluster with 35 processors (5 nodes). Because the simulation is not properly load balanced due to the equal-sized chunks, there is a large variation in the timings for different processors particularly for the DFT where there are several idle processors (i.e., chunks which do not contain any DFT pixels).\n\n\n![](images/parallel_benchmark_barplot.png#center)\n\n\nBased on these results, we plot the average of the *inverse* of the timings (proportional to the number of cycles per second; a \"rate\" quantity which can demonstrate linear scaling) for the time-stepping and DFT over the full range of cluster sizes. The time-stepping results demonstrate (approximately) linear scaling.  The size of the error bars increases with the number of cluster nodes mainly due to pronounced variations in the network bandwidth; the N1 instances do *not* support colocation via a [compact placement policy](https://cloud.google.com/solutions/best-practices-for-using-mpi-on-compute-engine). The DFT results (which excludes those processors without any DFT pixels) seem to be oscillating around a constant. This is not surprising because the processor(s) which takes the longest time to update its DFT pixels sets an upper bound on how fast the DFT calculation for all processors can proceed. It is the presence of this unique upper bound for each cluster which is revealed by the scaling plot.\n\nSee also [FAQ/Should I expect linear speedup from the parallel Meep](FAQ.md#should-i-expect-linear-speedup-from-the-parallel-meep)?\n\n\n![](images/parallel_benchmark_timestep.png#center)\n\n\n\n![](images/parallel_benchmark_DFT.png#center)\n\n\n\nDynamic Chunk Balancing\n-----------------------\n\nSince Meep's computation time is ultimately bottlenecked by the slowest-running process, it is desirable to load-balance the chunk layout such that each compute node is given an equal workload. By default, Meep uses a heuristics-based scheme to estimate the cost of a computation region based on the composition of voxel types (anisotropic, PML, etc.) However, this method of estimating the simulation time for a chunk in advance is not always accurate, a problem which is especially true for simulations run on shared-resource clusters. Meep's `chunk_balancer` module allows for a more empirical, data-driven approach for dynamically load-balancing parallel simulations. This approach uses the simulation time per node to adaptively modify the chunk layout and it implicitly corrects for heterogeneity over the simulation region and variability in background loads and job priority on shared compute resources. This approach can be especially useful for cases such as adjoint optimization, where slight variations on the same simulation are run many times over many iterations.\n\n\n![](images/adaptive_chunk_layout.gif#center)\n\n\n### Chunk balancer interface\n\nThe chunk balancer interface provides four main methods:\n- `make_initial_chunk_layout()` generates the initial chunk layout for the first iteration of a simulation. By default, `None` is returned, indicating Meep should use its default chunk partitioning strategy.\n- `should_adjust_chunk_layout()` decides whether the current layout is sufficiently poorly balanced to justify the up-front cost of reallocating the field arrays when changing chunk layouts.\n- `compute_new_chunk_layout()` looks at the current chunk layout and per-process timing data to compute a new chunk layout which has chunk sizes adjusted to improve the load balance across compute nodes.\n- `adjust_chunk_layout()` is syntactic sugar which will compute a new chunk layout, apply it to the simulation object, reset the simulation, and re-initialize the simulation.\n\n```py\nclass AbstractChunkBalancer(abc.ABC):\n  \"\"\"Chunk balancer for dynamically load-balanced chunk layouts.\"\"\"\n\n  def make_initial_chunk_layout(self, sim) -> mp.BinaryPartition:\n    \"\"\"Generates an initial chunk layout for simulation.\"\"\"\n\n  def should_adjust_chunk_layout(self, sim) -> bool:\n    \"\"\"Is current layout imbalanced enough to justify rebuilding sim?\"\"\"\n\n  @abc.abstractmethod\n  def compute_new_chunk_layout(\n    self,\n    timing_measurements: MeepTimingMeasurements,\n    old_chunk_layout: mp.BinaryPartition,\n    chunk_volumes: Tuple[mp.grid_volume],\n    chunk_owners: np.ndarray) -> mp.BinaryPartition:\n    \"\"\"Rebalance chunks to equalize simulation time for each node.\"\"\"\n\n  def adjust_chunk_layout(self, sim, **kwargs) -> None:\n    \"\"\"Computes a new chunk layout and applies it to sim.\"\"\"\n```\n\n### Usage\n\nUsing the chunk balancer is very straightforward, and it can typically be integrated into existing Meep simulations with only a few lines of code. Here is a simple example:\n\n```py\nfrom meep.chunk_balancer import ChunkBalancer\n\nchunk_balancer = ChunkBalancer()\n\n# Compute an initial chunk layout\ninitial_chunk_layout = chunk_balancer.make_initial_chunk_layout()\n\nsim = mp.Simulation(..., chunk_layout=initial_chunk_layout)\nsim.init_sim()\n\nfor iteration in range(epochs):\n  sim.run(...)\n  # Adjust the chunk layout for the next iteration if needed\n  chunk_balancer.adjust_chunk_layout(sim, sensitivity=0.4)\n```\n\nChunks can also be rebalanced between runs of a program by dumping and loading the chunk layout from a pickled object. For example:\n\n```py\nimport meep as mp\nfrom meep.chunk_balancer import ChunkBalancer\nfrom meep.timing_measurements import MeepTimingMeasurements\nimport pickle\nimport os.path\n\n# Fetch chunk layout from a previous run if it exists\nif os.path.exists(\"path/to/chunk_layout.pkl\"):\n  initial_chunk_layout = pickle.load(open(\"path/to/chunk_layout.pkl\", \"rb\"))\nelse:\n  initial_chunk_layout = None\n\nsim = mp.Simulation(..., chunk_layout=initial_chunk_layout)\nsim.init_sim()\nsim.run(...)\n\n# Compute and save chunk layout for next run\ntimings = MeepTimingMeasurements.new_from_simulation(sim)\nchunk_layout = sim.chunk_layout\nchunk_volumes = sim.structure.get_chunk_volumes()\nchunk_owners = sim.structure.get_chunk_owners()\nnext_chunk_layout = ChunkBalancer().compute_new_chunk_layout(\n    timings,\n    chunk_layout,\n    chunk_volumes,\n    chunk_owners,\n    sensitivity=0.4)\n\n# Save chunk layout for next run\nwith open(\"path/to/chunk_layout.pkl\", \"wb\") as f:\n    pickle.dump(next_chunk_layout, f)\n```\n\n### Chunk adjustment algorithm\n\nThe default chunk adjustment algorithm recursively traverses the `BinaryPartition` object and resizes the chunk volumes of the left and right children of each node to have an equal per-node simulation time. The new chunk layout has split positions which are a weighted average of the previous iteration's chunk layout and the newly computed layout, and the `sensitivity` parameter adjusts how fast the chunk sizes are adjusted. (`sensitivity=0.0` means no adjustment, `sensitivity=1.0` means an immediate snap to the predicted split positions, and `sensitivity=0.5` is the average of the old and new layouts.) The adjustment algorithm is summarized in pseudocode below:\n\n```\ndef adjust_split_pos(node):\n  for subtree in {node.left, node.right}:\n    V := Σ volume for nodes in subtree\n    t := Σ sim time for nodes in subtree\n    n := number of processes in subtree\n    l := t / n  # average load per process\n\n  Vₗ ↦ Vₗ / lₗ\n  Vᵣ ↦ Vᵣ / lᵣ\n\n  split_pos’ := dₘᵢₙ + (dₘₐₓ - dₘᵢₙ) * (Vₗ) / (Vₗ + Vᵣ)\n\n  # Adjust with sensitivity parameter\n  node.split_pos ↦ s * split_pos’ + (1-s) * node.split_pos\n\n  # Recurse through rest of the tree\n  adjust_split_pos(node.left)\n  adjust_split_pos(node.right)\n```\n\n### Load balancing results on shared clusters\n\nThe following benchmarking results show load-balancing improvements from a parallel run on a shared compute cluster in a datacenter. The per-core working times (blue and orange) start of initially poorly balanced using the default `split_by_cost` scheme, but the load balancing improves over successive iterations.\n\n\n![](images/chunk_balancer_timing_stats.gif#center)\n\n\nUsing the normalized standard deviation in simulation times per iteration as a proxy for load-balancing efficacy, we can see that the load balance improves over a large number of runs with varying numbers of processes:\n\n\n![](images/chunk_balancer_variance.jpg#center)\n","numLines":308,"startLine":1,"totalLines":308}}}
